about: Every rule qa/guess-sanity.mjs checks: what is checked, the line it must stay on, why, and the published source with its date. Written 2026-11-07 from the Survey of Consumer Finances 2025 public data and the other sources named per rule; a rule whose owner is a build (bought, leftover) is checked here and fixed there.

defs.home-debt: Shared terms: oldest = the adult with the highest age; ageAt(d) = oldest's age on date d; band = oldest's age band <35|35-44|45-54|55-64|65-74|75+; guessed(x) = x is a guess in plan.guesses or is worked out from any guessed input; typed(x) = in the plan and not a guess; M = the main mortgage as shown: M.owed, M.rate, M.pay (the shown monthly payment), M.esc = the tax+insurance inside M.pay (0 if the escrow tap is 'no'), M.pi = M.pay - M.esc, M.term = debts[].termMonths ?? 360, M.left = months left as a page shows it (balance/liabilities rows[].months, debt/mortgage), M.start = addMonths(today, M.left - M.term).
defs.spend-family: Shared terms (spending and family): H = the household as the plan holds it; adults = role self/partner, age(a) from birthDate at today; kids = dependents with an id setup-kid-* or under 18 (a dependent with no birth date counts as a kid of unknown age); fam = single | single+kids | couple | couple+kids (couple = two adults; +kids = a kid under 18 or of unknown age); gross = every income line active today, a year; fifth = the SCF 2025 income fifth of gross (cut-offs $35,946 / $63,676 / $102,703 / $174,595; a cell with fewer than 50 families, single+kids Q4 and Q5, widens to the neighbouring fifth); size = adults + dependents (5+ as 5). walk(H, taps) = Get started with every spending box left blank, saved as the screen saves it (setup spendArgs, estimate per row, applySpend with the guesses, then settle; qa/guess-sanity.mjs walk()). G.row = the grey figure saved for spend.<row>, a month; TOTAL = sum of G; LO = left over a month as Next best action, the Dashboard and Health score show it (next-best-action spare.monthly: after income and payroll tax); TH = after-tax income a month (spend.js takeHome a / 12). guessed(x) / typed(x) as docs/CONVENTIONS.md 'Guesses'. Grid = OH and CA x the four fam x gross $20k, 35k, 50k, 75k, 100k, 150k, 250k x oldest adult 25, 40, 60 x renter / owner without mortgage, one kid aged 8 with childcare 'no' (336 households: the spending grid the rules were written on; qa/guess-sanity.mjs runs a wider one).

rules.check: for each owned home whose purchase date P is guessed or derived (not typed): P <= today AND ageAt(P) >= 18. Also when M.start is derived: ageAt(home.purchaseDate) <= ageAt(M.start) (a loan or refinance never predates the purchase).
rules.threshold: ageAt(P) >= 18 (hard); P <= today; purchase <= loan start
rules.why: Nobody buys a home before adulthood and a mortgage cannot start before the home was bought. SCF 2025: among owners who bought their home (not inherited), only 0.4% report buying before 18 (family co-ownership); the 1st percentile of age at purchase is 20, the 5th 24. The SCF interview itself refuses a loan date before the purchase date (codebook edit check on X802 vs X720: 'LOAN/REFINANCE BEFORE PURCHASE DATE ERROR').
rules.source: Federal Reserve, Survey of Consumer Finances 2025 public data: X720 (year bought), X718 (bought vs inherited), X14/X19 (ages), X802 (year of current loan); https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt)
rules.sourceDate: 2025 SCF, released 2026-10-09; microdata computed 2026-11-07 (5 implicates, weight X42001, age band = oldest adult, as the app's profileOf)

rules.check: y = years between the guessed purchase date and today. Pass if SCF_YIH[band].p5 <= y <= SCF_YIH[band].p95. When nothing about the home's date or the mortgage's age is typed (no purchase date, no 'when taken out' tap, no term, not both owed and payment typed), the default must be central: SCF_YIH[band].p25 <= y <= SCF_YIH[band].p75.
rules.why: 'When people buy homes' for a household that already owns is the time since THEIR purchase at THEIR age, not the age of today's buyers. NAR 2026 (first-time buyers' median age 40, 38 for those who borrowed; repeat buyers 62; sellers' median stay 12 years) describes who buys now; a 25-year-old owner bought recently. SCF 2025 owners who bought: median years in the home 3 (<35), 5, 9, 14, 22, 24 (75+). Census ACS 2025 agrees: 75.3% of owner householders under 35 moved in 2020 or later and 96.4% in 2010 or later.
rules.source: SCF 2025 microdata (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt)); Census ACS 2025 1-year B25128 Tenure by Age of Householder by Year Moved In, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2025/table-based-SF/data/1YRData/acsdt1y2025-b25128.dat (U.S. row); NAR 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers news release, https://www.nar.realtor/newsroom/first-time-home-buyer-share-inches-up-to-22-median-age-remains-at-record-high-of-40
rules.sourceDate: SCF released 2026-10-09; ACS 2025 files posted 2026-10-29; NAR released 2026-11-05; all read 2026-11-07

rules.check: If any of M.owed, M.pay, M.rate, M.left is guessed: 0 < M.left <= M.term AND M.start <= today AND ageAt(M.start) >= 18 (oldest adult; the youngest borrower if only one adult is named on the loan) AND (home.purchaseDate unknown OR M.start >= home.purchaseDate). M.left is the figure each page shows, so run it on balance/liabilities, debt/mortgage and the estimator (overview/guesses) separately.
rules.threshold: M.left in (0, M.term]; ageAt(M.start) >= 18; M.start >= purchase date
rules.why: The owner's example: a 25-year-old couple shown about 12 years left on a 30-year loan means the loan began when they were 7. SCF 2025: among mortgage holders under 35 only 3.0% have 12 years or less left, and the 1st percentile of the oldest adult's age when the current loan began is 23 (5th: 26). Today this fails: with nothing typed, Debts and Mortgage run the guessed payment, which includes property tax and insurance, as if it were all principal and interest, so a 22-year-old single on $40k is shown 177 months (payoff 2041-08, loan begun about age 7) and a 25-year-old couple 211 months (begun about 13).
rules.source: SCF 2025 microdata X802 (year current loan taken or refinanced), X806 (term), X14/X19; https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt)
rules.sourceDate: 2025 SCF, released 2026-10-09; microdata computed 2026-11-07 (5 implicates, weight X42001, age band = oldest adult, as the app's profileOf)

rules.check: If M.left is guessed or derived from a guess: ageAt(M.start) >= 22; same for the guessed home purchase date: ageAt(purchaseDate) >= 22.
rules.threshold: >= 22 years old when the current loan began or the home was bought
rules.why: Outside the middle 90%: SCF 2025 5th percentile of the oldest adult's age when the current mortgage began is 22 for owners under 35 (26 for all); 5th percentile of age at purchase is 24 for all owners who bought. FHFA NMDB: only 6.1% of 2025 home-purchase loan borrowers were under 25.
rules.source: SCF 2025 microdata (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt)); FHFA National Mortgage Database, New Residential Mortgage Statistics, annual national file, 2025, market 'All Mortgages (Home Purchase)', series PCT_AGE_LT25 / AVE_AGE_BORROWER (41), https://www.fhfa.gov/document/d/nmdb/nmdb-new-mortgage-statistics-national-census-areas-annual.zip
rules.sourceDate: SCF released 2026-10-09; NMDB files released 2026-09-30 (data through 2025 / 2026 Q2); read 2026-11-07

rules.check: yl = M.left / 12 as shown. If guessed(yl): SCF_LEFT[band].p5 <= yl <= SCF_LEFT[band].p95. If nothing that fixes the loan's age is typed (no 'when taken out' tap, purchase date, term or start date, and not both M.owed and M.pay typed): SCF_LEFT[band].p25 <= yl <= SCF_LEFT[band].p75.
rules.why: Years left on a mortgage fall with age: SCF 2025 median years left 27 (<35) down to 17 (75+). FHFA NMDB 2026 Q2: average loan age 80 months, only 27.8% of loans are 4 years old or less, 20.2% are over 10, and 83.1% are 30-year fixed. Today the estimator pays every guessed balance over a fresh 360 months at every age (above the 75th percentile in every band and above the 95th from 45 on), while the pages show 14 to 18 years because of the escrow mix-up (HD-AMORT-IDENTITY).
rules.source: SCF 2025 microdata X802, X806 (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt)); FHFA NMDB Outstanding Residential Mortgage Statistics, national quarterly, 2026Q2, series AVE_AGE_LOAN, PCT_TENURE_*, PCT_TERM_FRM_30, https://www.fhfa.gov/document/d/nmdb/nmdb-outstanding-mortgage-statistics-national-census-areas-quarterly.zip (definitions: https://www.fhfa.gov/document/d/nmdb/nmdb-aggregate-statistics-data-dictionary-technical-notes-2026q1.pdf)
rules.sourceDate: SCF released 2026-10-09; NMDB released 2026-09-30 (data through 2026 Q2); read 2026-11-07

rules.check: Sweep: one household (Ohio, couple, $90,000 pay each, owns with a mortgage picked, nothing typed about the home or loan), both birth years moved so the oldest is 22..85 by 1. Let L(a) = guessed years left, Y(a) = guessed years in the home, V(a) = guessed mortgage owed / guessed home value. Require L non-increasing, Y non-decreasing, V non-increasing in a (tolerance 0.5 year / 0.01), and L(30) - L(78) >= 5, Y(78) - Y(30) >= 10.
rules.threshold: non-increasing years left and owed/value, non-decreasing years in home; drops of >= 5 years left and >= 10 years in home between 30 and 78
rules.why: SCF 2025 medians by oldest adult's band (<35 to 75+): years left 27, 26, 24, 23, 21, 17; years in home 3, 5, 9, 14, 22, 24; owed/value 0.73, 0.54, 0.44, 0.40, 0.32, 0.25. The published tables show the same fall: median mortgage 218.5k, 215k, 203k, 165k, 130k, 100k over median home 320k, 376k, 400k, 400k, 382k, 350k. Today L(a) = 30 for every age, so the 30-vs-78 drop is 0.
rules.source: SCF 2025 microdata (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt)); SCF 2025 tables, Table 9 and Alternate Table 13 (2025 medians), https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025_tables_internal_real_historical.xlsx
rules.sourceDate: 2025 SCF, released 2026-10-09; microdata computed 2026-11-07 (5 implicates, weight X42001, age band = oldest adult, as the app's profileOf)

rules.check: Sweep: one household (oldest 45, Ohio, owns with a mortgage, nothing typed about the home or loan), household pay $30,000..$400,000 in $10,000 steps. Guessed home value and guessed mortgage owed are non-decreasing in pay (tolerance 1%).
rules.threshold: non-decreasing in pay
rules.why: SCF 2025 medians by income percentile (0-20, 20-40, 40-60, 60-80, 80-90, 90-100): home value 150k, 250k, 350k, 375k, 525k, 910k; mortgage owed 51.3k, 119k, 144.1k, 188k, 275k, 400k: both rise at every step.
rules.source: SCF 2025 tables, Table 9 (2025 %s & medians, Primary residence) and Alternate Table 13 (2025 %s & median, Mortgages), https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025_tables_internal_real_historical.xlsx
rules.sourceDate: file last modified 2026-10-09; read 2026-11-07

rules.check: If guessed(M.owed) or guessed(home.value): M.owed <= home.value (typed or guessed). If home.value is typed, a guessed M.owed never exceeds it.
rules.threshold: owed / value <= 1.00
rules.why: A default must never put a household underwater. FHFA NMDB 2026 Q2: 0.3% of U.S. mortgages have a current loan-to-value above 100%; SCF 2025: 0.65% of mortgage holders owe more than they say the home would sell for.
rules.source: FHFA NMDB Outstanding Residential Mortgage Statistics, national quarterly, 2026Q2, series PCT_MTMLTV_GT100, https://www.fhfa.gov/document/d/nmdb/nmdb-outstanding-mortgage-statistics-national-census-areas-quarterly.zip; SCF 2025 microdata X805/X716 (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt))
rules.sourceDate: NMDB released 2026-09-30; SCF released 2026-10-09; read 2026-11-07

rules.check: r = M.owed / home.value where at least one is guessed. Pass if r <= SCF_LTV[band].p95; when neither owed nor value nor payment is typed, SCF_LTV[band].p25 <= r <= SCF_LTV[band].p75.
rules.why: Owed-to-value falls with age as loans are paid down and homes gain value; FHFA NMDB 2026 Q2: only 4.7% of loans are above 90% of the home's value. Current guesses pass (25-year-old couple 0.72, 60-year-old couple 0.44, 78-year-old 0.21).
rules.source: SCF 2025 microdata X805 (owed), X716 (value) (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt)); FHFA NMDB 2026Q2 PCT_MTMLTV_91_100 and _GT100
rules.sourceDate: 2025 SCF, released 2026-10-09; microdata computed 2026-11-07 (5 implicates, weight X42001, age band = oldest adult, as the app's profileOf)

rules.check: If guessed(M.rate) and y = year(M.start) >= 1996: d = M.rate*100 - PMMS30[y] (Freddie Mac annual average of the weekly 30-year rate). Pass if -2.84 <= d <= +1.46. When nothing about the loan's date or rate is typed: -1.04 <= d <= +0.16.
rules.why: A loan's rate is set in the year it starts. SCF 2025: for 30-year loans, rate minus Freddie Mac's average for the loan's year has p5 -2.84, p25 -1.04, median -0.26, p75 +0.16, p95 +1.46 points; loans taken in 2023 or later have a median rate of 6.25%. Today a guessed loan with 30 years left (begun 2026) carries the 4.6% average of old loans (FHFA NMDB 2026 Q2 average 4.4%), 1.9 points under 2026's 6.53%.
rules.source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey weekly history, column pmms30, https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms/docs/PMMS_history.csv (latest week 2026-11-05: 7.18%); SCF 2025 microdata X816 (rate), X802 (year), X806 (term) (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt))
rules.sourceDate: PMMS through 2026-11-05, read 2026-11-07; SCF released 2026-10-09

rules.check: For every debt row with owed > 0 on every page that shows it: pi = pay - esc (esc = M.esc for the mortgage, 0 otherwise); pi > owed*rate/12 (the payment covers the month's interest); months = nper(rate/12, pi, owed) and the shown months left / payoff date equal ceil(months) +/- 1; for a guessed payment, pmt(rate/12, left, owed) + esc rounds to the shown payment (+/- the guess rounding) AND left <= term. The months a page shows must be computed from pi, never from the payment that includes tax and insurance.
rules.threshold: +/- 1 month; +/- $1 or the guess rounding step; pi > interest
rules.why: Payment, balance, rate and months left are one equation; any page that breaks it shows a date that is plain wrong. SCF 2025: 56.0% of mortgage payments include both property tax and insurance (6.8% tax only, 3.4% insurance only, 33.8% neither), so the escrow part is common and must be taken out before working out months left. Today balance/liabilities and debt/mortgage run nper on the full guessed payment (25-year-old couple: $1,800 with $1,333 principal and interest, shown 211 months instead of 360); the estimator's rounding also puts a 22-year-old's loan at 367 months, past its 360-month term.
rules.source: SCF 2025 microdata X810 ('Does this amount include real estate taxes or homeowners' insurance?') (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt)); amortisation arithmetic (core/math/finance.js pmt / nper)
rules.sourceDate: 2025 SCF, released 2026-10-09; microdata computed 2026-11-07 (5 implicates, weight X42001, age band = oldest adult, as the app's profileOf)

rules.check: tax_home = property tax a year on property/home; ins_home = home insurance a year there. If the mortgage payment includes escrow: M.esc*12 == tax_home + ins_home (+/- $12), and cashflow/expenses (and the left-over figure on Dashboard / Forecast) count tax and insurance once: not as their own lines AND inside the mortgage payment. When the escrow tap is unanswered, the payment is treated as including both.
rules.threshold: +/- $1 a month; counted exactly once
rules.why: One figure across pages, counted once. SCF 2025: 56.0% of mortgage payers say the payment includes both tax and insurance, the most likely answer, so 'not sure' means included; the other 44% pay them apart, so a page that adds them again on top of an escrowed payment overstates spending and understates what is left over.
rules.source: SCF 2025 microdata X810 (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt))
rules.sourceDate: 2025 SCF, released 2026-10-09; microdata computed 2026-11-07 (5 implicates, weight X42001, age band = oldest adult, as the app's profileOf)

rules.check: When debts[<mortgage>].escrowMonthly is our guess (estimator debt.mortgage.escrow: a guessed payment kept, or the escrow question answered Not sure / Yes with no figure): 0 < escrow <= payment / 2; payment - escrow > the month's interest (owed x rate / 12); the loan is paid off within 360 months at payment - escrow (a guessed figure never stretches a loan past 30 years: fix round 1, 2026-11-11); escrow <= (the guessed property tax a year + the guessed home insurance a year) / 12; and escrow x 12 / home value within the sum of HD-PROPTAX's and HD-HOMEINS's bands (0.32%..4.11% a year; only the top of the band when the payment's room cut the figure below the usual one).
rules.threshold: at most half the payment; leaves more than the interest; at most the usual tax and insurance (+$1); 0.32%..4.11% of the home's value a year
rules.why: The tax and insurance inside the payment come out of it before the loan is paid: too large a figure makes the loan look like it never ends, too small one makes the payoff too early. A guessed figure is the usual tax and insurance for the home's value and state, never more than half the payment.
rules.source: SCF 2025 microdata X810 (whether the payment includes tax and insurance: 56.0% yes) https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip; sizes as HD-PROPTAX (Census ACS 2025 1-year B25103/B25077, AHS 2023 PUF PROTAXAMT) and HD-HOMEINS (AHS 2023 PUF INSURAMT)
rules.sourceDate: SCF 2025 released 2026-10-09; ACS 2025 files posted 2026-10-29; AHS 2023 PUF dated 2025-01-22; all computed 2026-11-07

rules.check: t = property tax a year / home value, when either is guessed. Pass if 0.0022 <= t <= 0.025. When the tax is guessed: t equals the state's ACS rate (median tax / median value) +/- 1%, and with no state the U.S. 0.90%.
rules.threshold: 0.22%..2.5% of value (AHS p5..p95); state rates 0.26% (Hawaii) to 1.92% (Illinois), U.S. 0.90%
rules.why: AHS 2023 owners: property tax as a share of the home's value p5 0.22%, p25 0.58%, median 0.89%, p75 1.43%, p95 2.5%. ACS 2025: median real estate taxes over median value range from 0.26% (Hawaii) to 1.92% (Illinois), U.S. 0.90% ($3,344 on $371,100).
rules.source: Census American Housing Survey 2023 national PUF v1.1, household.csv PROTAXAMT (monthly), MARKETVAL, TENURE=1, WEIGHT, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/ahs/2023/AHS%202023%20National%20PUF%20v1.1%20CSV.zip; Census ACS 2025 1-year B25103 (median real estate taxes) and B25077 (median value), https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2025/table-based-SF/data/1YRData/acsdt1y2025-b25103.dat and .../acsdt1y2025-b25077.dat
rules.sourceDate: AHS 2023 PUF file dated 2025-01-22; ACS 2025 files posted 2026-10-29; both computed 2026-11-07

rules.check: i = home insurance a year / home value, when either is guessed. Pass if 0.0010 <= i <= 0.0161.
rules.threshold: 0.10%..1.61% of value a year (AHS p5..p95; median 0.41%)
rules.why: AHS 2023 owners: insurance a year over value p5 0.10%, p25 0.27%, median 0.41%, p75 0.52%, p95 1.61%. The guess is the state's average premium whatever the home is worth, so it can fall outside for a very cheap or very dear home; current guesses (0.31% to 0.80%) pass.
rules.source: Census American Housing Survey 2023 national PUF v1.1, household.csv INSURAMT (monthly), MARKETVAL, TENURE=1, WEIGHT, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/ahs/2023/AHS%202023%20National%20PUF%20v1.1%20CSV.zip
rules.sourceDate: AHS 2023 PUF file dated 2025-01-22; computed 2026-11-07

rules.check: If guessed(home.value) and household gross income I >= $1,000 a year (below it the ratio bounds nothing: the lowest point of the survey income scale the estimators use): SCF_VI[band].p5 <= home.value / I <= SCF_VI[band].p95. If purchase price and year are typed: home.value == price * HPI[state][now] / HPI[state][year] (+/- 1%).
rules.why: SCF 2025 owners' home value over family income by the oldest adult's age band; retirees' ratios are wide because income drops while the home stays. Current guesses pass (22-year-old on $40k: $160k = 4.0; 78-year-old on $30k: $150k = 5.0).
rules.source: SCF 2025 microdata X716 (value), X5729 (income) (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt))
rules.sourceDate: 2025 SCF, released 2026-10-09; microdata computed 2026-11-07 (5 implicates, weight X42001, age band = oldest adult, as the app's profileOf)

rules.check: For a car loan with owed > 0 where owed, payment or rate is guessed: 1 <= months left <= 96, payoff date after this month, and months left <= the term the app assumes (Experian average for new or used).
rules.threshold: 1..96 months left
rules.why: Car loans longer than 8 years are almost non-existent: SCF 2025 vehicle loans with terms over 8 years are 0.5%; the Federal Reserve G.19 average maturity on new-car loans at finance companies is 67 months.
rules.source: SCF 2025 microdata X2208/X2308 (year taken), X2212/X2312 (years), X2218/X2318 (owed) (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt)); Federal Reserve G.19 Consumer Credit, Terms of Credit, release of 2026-11-06, https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/current/default.htm
rules.sourceDate: SCF released 2026-10-09; G.19 released 2026-11-06; read 2026-11-07

rules.check: m = months left on a car loan worked out from any guessed input. Pass if m <= 72 and owed / payment <= 60. When neither the 'when you got it' tap nor the payment is typed: 24 <= m <= 48.
rules.threshold: <= 72 months (p95); default 24..48 (p25..p75); owed/payment <= 60 months (p95)
rules.why: SCF 2025 vehicle loans: years left p5 0, p25 2, median 3, p75 4, p95 6; owed divided by the monthly payment p95 60 months; loan term median 5 years, p95 7. Current guesses (about 34 months) pass.
rules.source: SCF 2025 microdata X2208, X2212, X2213 with frequency X7537, X2218 (and vehicle 2) (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt))
rules.sourceDate: 2025 SCF, released 2026-10-09; microdata computed 2026-11-07 (5 implicates, weight X42001, age band = oldest adult, as the app's profileOf)

rules.check: For a student loan with owed > 0 where owed, payment or rate is guessed: payment > owed*rate/12 AND 1 <= nper(rate/12, payment, owed) <= 360 AND payoff date after this month.
rules.threshold: pays the interest; <= 360 months left
rules.why: No federal plan runs past 30 years: Standard pays off in 10 years, 10 to 30 for consolidation loans; the Tiered Standard plan for loans made from July 1, 2026 is 10, 15, 20 or 25 years by amount borrowed; the Repayment Assistance Plan forgives what is left after 30 years of payments. SCF 2025: owed over the monthly payment has median 80 months and p95 333.
rules.source: Edfinancial Services (a U.S. Department of Education loan servicer), 'Lower Payment Options', https://edfinancial.studentaid.gov/lower-payment-options; SCF 2025 microdata X7824 (owed), X7815/X7816 (payment) (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt))
rules.sourceDate: servicer page (c) 2026 with a 2026-07-01 notice, read 2026-11-07; SCF released 2026-10-09

rules.check: If the card minimum is guessed: min = (b <= $40 ? b : max(40, 0.01*b + b*apr/12)) rounded as the guess rounds, and min <= b; therefore min > b*apr/12 and the payoff at the minimum (paying min recomputed each month) is finite. Shown months to pay off at the minimum <= 360 for b <= $29,000.
rules.threshold: min = higher of $40 or 1% + the month's interest, never above the balance; payoff at the minimum <= 360 months for balances up to $29,000
rules.why: CFPB (December 2025): issuers set the minimum at the highest of a dollar floor (most often $40, range $15 to $50) or about 1% of the balance plus interest and fees; about 15% of general-purpose cardholders paid only the minimum in 2024. At the G.19 card rate of 22.36% this pays off $3,000 in 134 months and $29,000 (SCF p95 balance among carriers) in 359 months; a guessed minimum below the interest would show a debt that never ends.

rules.source: SCF 2025 microdata X413/X421/X427, X5729 (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scf2025s.zip (p25i6.dta; codebook https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2025.txt))

'Debt-free' on timeline and projection == max(payoffMonth) over live debts. A page that shows a second date (with extra, a strategy) labels it.

rules.check: For every debt and the home, with g = a guessed figure and t = typed ones: (a) typed home value V: guessed M.owed <= V and guessed tax/insurance scale from V; (b) typed payment P and owed B, guessed rate r: r < 12*(P - esc)/B (the typed payment covers the guessed rate's interest) and nper(r/12, P-esc, B) <= M.term; (c) typed owed B, guessed payment: pmt over the guessed months left with M.start >= typed purchase date; (d) typed purchase date, term, start date or 'when taken out' tap: the guess uses them (years in home and months left follow from them, not from the band default); (e) typed property tax or insurance on Home: the escrow inside a guessed payment uses them; (f) every guess is unchanged when an unrelated typed figure is re-saved with the same value.

rules.why: Standing rule: a guess fills a blank and never overrides or contradicts what the person typed; HD-MORT-START and HD-AMORT-IDENTITY are the arithmetic each pairing must satisfy.
rules.source: docs/CONVENTIONS.md 'Guesses' (a guess is an ordinary value plus a ledger entry; typed figures win)

rules.threshold: S <= G (hard); leftover from guesses alone >= -10% of take-home
rules.why: Guessed payments alone that use up all of a household's pay are nonsense as a default; a household that typed nothing has no reason to be shown in the red.
rules.source: SCF 2025 summary extract, PIRTOTAL (ratio of debt payments to income), https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scfp2025s.zip

rules.check: for a in H.adults where a.status == 'work': payYear(a) = sum(inc.items where personId==a.id and type in ['salary','business'] and active).yearly; ASSERT payYear(a) > 0 AND (pc.people has a.id when the pay is a salary) AND ss.people[a.id].source != 'none' (unless a.ssMode in ['none','statement']) AND, for a married pair, ss.couple.spousalCounted is computed from a figure, not from 'none'. A blank pay box is filled by a marked guess (the pay estimator planned as E33/E34), never left at $0.
rules.threshold: payYear > 0 for every adult the household said works; the guess itself must satisfy pt.pay.guess-by-age
rules.why: Saying 'I work' and then being counted on $0 of pay contradicts something typed. Most full-time workers earn far above $0: the lowest tenth of full-time wage and salary workers earn under $642 a week (about $33,400 a year), the median $1,251 a week; in married-couple families both spouses work in 49.1% (66.3% with children), so a second earner left at $0 is the common case, not a rare one.
rules.source: BLS, Usual Weekly Earnings of Wage and Salary Workers, Table 5 (quartiles and deciles), 2nd quarter 2026, https://www.bls.gov/news.release/wkyeng.t05.htm ; BLS, Employment Characteristics of Families 2025 (USDL-26-0652), https://www.bls.gov/news.release/famee.nr0.htm
rules.skeptic: 2026-11-07: Social Security cannot be estimated without a birth year (the page asks for it): required only once the person has one.

rules.check: when pay is a guess (ledger entry on an income amount): weekly = guessYearly/52; band = BLS age band of the person (16-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65+); ASSERT weekly within ±10% of the band median (16-24 $773, 25-34 $1,173, 35-44 $1,414, 45-54 $1,407, 55-64 $1,376, 65+ $1,165) times any state/part-time factor the estimator documents; MONOTONE: for the same household with only the age changed, guess(16-24) < guess(25-34) < guess(35-44) and guess(55-64) >= guess(65+) and guess(45-54) >= guess(65+) (the hump).
rules.threshold: ±10% of the BLS age-band median; inside BLS P10..P90 ($642..$2,924 a week) always
rules.why: Pay by age follows a hump: full-time medians rise from $773 a week at 16-24 to $1,414 at 35-44, stay near $1,407 at 45-54 and $1,376 at 55-64, and fall to $1,165 at 65+. A guess that gives a 22-year-old the pay of a 45-year-old, or that is flat across ages, is not the most likely figure for that person.
rules.source: BLS, Usual Weekly Earnings, Table 3 (median usual weekly earnings of full-time wage and salary workers by age), 3rd quarter 2026, https://www.bls.gov/news.release/wkyeng.t03.htm ; Table 5 deciles, https://www.bls.gov/news.release/wkyeng.t05.htm

If a raise is ever guessed: guessRaise(16-24) >= guessRaise(25-54) >= guessRaise(55+) (non-increasing in age).
rules.threshold: Projection vs Salary page within $1; Income's figure only when a raise is typed (skeptic pass 2026-11-07; was: |difference| <= $1 a year between pages, after the real/nominal conversion)
rules.why: One person's pay next year is one figure. The population's raise falls with age: the median 12-month wage growth of the same workers was 6.5% at 16-24, 3.9% at 25-54 and 2.9% at 55+ (overall 3.7%, 12-month averages to September 2026), so 0% on one page and 3% on another is wrong on at least one page for everyone, and a flat raise overstates it for older workers.
rules.source: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Wage Growth Tracker (wage-growth-data.xlsx, sheet 'Age', 12-month moving averages, 16-24 / 25-54 / 55+), https://www.atlantafed.org/research-and-data/data/wage-growth-tracker
rules.sourceDate: 2026-10-08 (data through September 2026)
rules.skeptic: 2026-11-07: With no raise typed, Income's 'Next year' is this year's pay labelled 'no raises entered': a statement of what was typed, not a forecast. The forecasts (Projection, Salary) are held to one path.

rules.check: for a in H.adults where a.status == 'work' and a has an active pay line today: retireAge(a) = a.retirementAge ?? plan.assumptions.retirementAge; ASSERT proj.inputs.people[a].retireAge > a.age (a default already passed becomes floor(a.age)+1, as applyAges does for a typed one) AND proj.rows[0] (this year) counts a's pay (rows[0].retired == false while anyone still works, or the year's pay prorated) AND the Social Security start used for a is pt.ss.claim-age's age, not a past one.
rules.threshold: no working adult is retired in a past or current year by a default; pay counted in this year's row
rules.why: A person who says they work and has pay on Income is working now; retiring them in the past contradicts what they typed. Working past 65 is common: 5.8 million full-time wage and salary workers are 65 or older (median $1,165 a week).
rules.source: BLS, Usual Weekly Earnings, Table 3, 3rd quarter 2026 (65 years and over: 5,818 thousand full-time workers), https://www.bls.gov/news.release/wkyeng.t03.htm

rules.check: for p in pc.people (W-2 pay): base = Social Security wage base for pc.year (2026 $184,500; 2027 $192,300); ASSERT |p.yearly.ss - 0.062*min(p.wages.fica*paychecks, base)| <= 1 AND |p.yearly.medicare - (0.0145*ficaWages + 0.009*max(0, ficaWages - 200000))| <= 1 AND p.yearly.net <= p.yearly.gross - p.yearly.ss - p.yearly.medicare AND 0 < p.yearly.net/p.yearly.gross <= 0.9235 (below the base, before any other deduction) AND th.monthly == inc.monthly - th.salaryGrossMonthly + th.salaryNetMonthly. MONOTONE: sweep the person's pay from $5,000 to $400,000 in $2,500 steps with everything else fixed: net take-home never falls as pay rises.
rules.threshold: $1 a year on each payroll line; net(pay + 2,500) >= net(pay) - $0.50
rules.why: Employee payroll tax is fixed by law: 6.2% Social Security up to the year's taxable maximum ($184,500 in 2026, $192,300 in 2027) and 1.45% Medicare on all wages, plus 0.9% that the employer withholds on wages over $200,000 in the year whatever the filing status. Take-home that falls when pay rises is never true for a paycheck.
rules.source: SSA, 2026 and 2027 COLA fact sheets (tax rates and maximum taxable earnings), https://www.ssa.gov/cola/factsheets/2026.html and https://www.ssa.gov/cola/factsheets/2027.html ; IRS Topic 751, https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc751

rules.check: code = H.state; if code not in NO_WAGE_TAX (AK FL NV NH SD TN TX WY, and WA wages) and household wages+business+pension > the state's own zero line (its 2026 standard deduction/exemptions: e.g. CA $5,540 single, NY $8,000, GA $12,000/$24,000): ASSERT st.tax > 0 AND st.method != 'unknown' (a marked guess from the state's 2026 brackets, or the survey ratio spend.js already uses) AND sum(pc.people.yearly.state) > 0 AND th.monthly < (same plan with st.tax forced to 0).th.monthly AND side.setAside.state > 0 when side income > 0. ONE FIGURE: st.tax == spend.js takeHome(plan).state (when both use the same method) and sum(pc.people.yearly.state) == st.tax * (state wages / st.agi) within $1. If code is in NO_WAGE_TAX: every page's state income tax on wages == 0.
rules.threshold: state tax > 0 above the state's zero line; the pages agree within $1 a year
rules.why: 41 states and D.C. tax wages in 2026 (15 flat, 26 graduated plus D.C.); only AK, FL, NV, NH, SD, TN, TX, WY have no income tax and WA taxes capital gains only. A $0 state tax for a $70,000 earner in California (about $2,390 a year at the 2026 brackets) or Georgia (5.19% flat) is impossible, and it overstates take-home and the left-over figure every month.
rules.source: Tax Foundation, 2026 State Individual Income Tax Rates and Brackets (structures table and rates/brackets as of January 1, 2026), https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/state/state-income-tax-rates-2026/

rules.check: if any adult has relation 'partner' (not 'spouse'): ASSERT H.filingStatus not in ['married_joint','married_separate'] AND fed (known() total, as Withholding check reads it) == sum over each partner of federalTax(own wages, own business, own other income, own dependents, status single or head_of_household) within $1 AND ans.totalTax equals that sum AND the verdict compares it with ans.projected. For a married couple ('spouse'), the default is married_joint.
rules.threshold: $1 a year
rules.why: Only a married couple can file one joint return; an unmarried person files their own return as single (or head of household with a qualifying child), so two unmarried partners file two returns. Putting both pays on one single return pushes the second pay into higher brackets and invents a tax bill.
rules.source: IRS Publication 501 (2025), Filing Status: 'You can choose married filing jointly as your filing status if you are considered married'; 'Your filing status is single if you are considered unmarried', https://www.irs.gov/publications/p501
rules.sourceDate: 2025 returns edition (read 2026-11-07)
rules.skeptic: 2026-11-07: Compares the figure the Federal estimate shows (fullSteps total over known.js: the 401(k) put in from pay comes off wages), for the household and for each partner's own return, not result.totalTax.
rules.verify: 2026-11-07: each partner's own return holds this year's 401(k) and IRA draw for spending at $0 (alone, a partner keeps the household's bills and the estimate drew them all from their own 401(k), with the 10% before 59 1/2); when the household itself draws, its figure is compared with that draw held at $0 too. The children may go with either partner: the page passes if it matches either way round. Without this, 32 grid households failed with the page below two returns.

rules.check: if ans.from == 'paycheck' (no per-paycheck figure and no year-so-far typed for anyone) and the household's income is W-2 pay only (no business line, no side income, taxable other income < $1,500, no stock vesting): ASSERT NOT (ans.balance >= 1000 AND ans.projected < 0.90 * ans.totalTax). For a married_joint couple where both have pay, the default W-4 for each job is Step 2(c) ticked (or the two-jobs worksheet result), i.e. ans.projected within ±10% of ans.totalTax before credits on the W-4 Step 3. Single earner: unchanged.
rules.threshold: no guessed bill of $1,000+ with under 90% withheld for a W-2-only household
rules.why: The 2026 Form W-4 tells a married-filing-jointly worker whose spouse also works to complete Step 2 (the estimator, the worksheet, or the box on both W-4s); withholding then lands near the tax. In 2025, 62.6% of returns got a refund (103.8 million of 165.8 million, average $3,167), and only about 9.5% were assessed the estimated-tax penalty (15.7 million penalties on individual and estate/trust returns in FY2025) — owing $1,000+ with under 90% withheld is outside the middle 90%. Both spouses work in 49.1% of married-couple families, so this default is hit by half of couples.
rules.source: IRS Form W-4 (2026), Step 2, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/fw4.pdf ; IRS 2025 filing season statistics, week ending Dec. 26, 2025, https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/filing-season-statistics-for-week-ending-dec-26-2025 ; IRS Data Book FY2025 Table 4-2 (estimated tax penalties, individual), https://www.irs.gov/statistics/soi-tax-stats-civil-penalties-assessed-and-abated-by-type-of-tax-and-type-of-penalty-irs-data-book-table-4-2 ; IRS Topic 306 ($1,000 and 90%), https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc306
rules.sourceDate: W-4 created 2025-12-08; filing stats 2025-12-26; Data Book FY2025; Topic 306 reviewed 2026-09-24
rules.skeptic: 2026-11-07: Failures are split by household: unmarried partners (the bill comes from one return for both: pt.tax.partners-two-returns) and married two earners (each W-4 left at married filing jointly without Step 2).

rules.check: a = ans (taxes/withholding taxAnswer); ASSERT est.balanceAtFiling == a.balance (±$1) AND overview/quick 'What will I owe' headline amount == |a.balance| with the same verdict AND overview/alerts 'tax-bill' amount == the owing returns' balances AND the federal page's known() total == a.totalTax AND verdict == 'owe' iff a.balance >= the verdict line, 'refund' iff a.balance <= -line AND 0 <= a.projected <= sum of gross pay + withheld retirement withdrawals AND est.needsEstimates implies a.balance >= 1000.

rules.why: The bill or refund in April is one number; the underpayment rules it rests on are fixed: generally no penalty when the balance after withholding is under $1,000, or when withholding and estimates cover 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's (110% above $150,000 AGI).
rules.source: IRS Topic 306, Penalty for underpayment of estimated tax, https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc306
rules.sourceDate: 2026-09-24 (page reviewed)
rules.skeptic: 2026-11-07: The Federal estimate page shows fullSteps' total (taxes/federal view.js full.total), the same figure as Withholding check; result.totalTax is the answer keys' return and is not on screen. The first sweep compared result.totalTax and failed 1,129 households on a figure no page shows.

rules.check: for each person with business/side profit P (side.items, Income type business) and W-2 wages W in the year: base = wage base(year); se = 0.9235*P >= 400 ? 0.124*min(0.9235*P, max(0, base - W)) + 0.029*0.9235*P + 0.009*max(0, W + 0.9235*P - addlThreshold(filing)) : 0; ASSERT side.setAside.yearly >= se AND side.setAside.rate * P <= P*(0.153 + 0.37 + topStateRate(H.state)) AND (H.state taxes wages and P > 0 implies side.setAside.state > 0, pt.state.never-silent-zero) AND the Self-employment page's se.total == se within $1.
rules.threshold: set-aside at least the self-employment tax; state part never $0 in a state that taxes wages
rules.why: Self-employment tax is 15.3% (12.4% Social Security up to the wage base less W-2 wages, 2.9% Medicare) on 92.35% of net earnings, owed once net earnings reach $400; the extra 0.9% Medicare starts at $200,000 ($250,000 joint, $125,000 separate). Setting aside less than that, or no state tax in a state that taxes it, guarantees a bill the page did not warn about.
rules.source: IRS Topic 554, Self-employment tax, https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc554 ; SSA 2026 COLA fact sheet (self-employed 15.30%, maximum taxable earnings $184,500), https://www.ssa.gov/cola/factsheets/2026.html

rules.check: for a in H.adults: fra = FRA(a.birthYear) per SSA (1943-54: 66; 1955 66y2m; 1956 66y4m; 1957 66y6m; 1958 66y8m; 1959 66y10m; 1960+: 67; born January 1 counts as the year before); if not ss.people[a].claimed and no claimAge typed: want = clamp(max(fra, ceilToMonth(a.age)), 62, 70); ASSERT ss.people[a].claimAge == want AND ss.people[a].fromAge >= floor(a.age) AND the monthly counted == benefit at want (delayed credits included) AND scenarios/compare get(), scenarios/goal-seek claims, the projection's Social Security start and the timeline mark all use want (no literal 67). Claimed: claimAge <= a.age. Always 62 <= claimAge <= 70 except a benefit marked paidUnreduced (disability or survivor).
rules.threshold: exact to the month
rules.why: Full retirement age is fixed by birth year: 66 for people born 1943-54, rising to 67 for those born in 1960 or later. A benefit not yet claimed cannot start in the past; someone past full retirement age who has not claimed earns delayed credits until they do (to 70). 67 as a fallback is wrong for everyone born before 1960.
rules.source: SSA, Cost-of-Living Increase and Other Determinations for 2026, Federal Register 2025-19763 ('The NRA is age 66 for those born in 1943-54. It gradually increases to age 67 for those born in 1960 or later'), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-11-03/pdf/2025-19763.pdf
rules.skeptic: 2026-11-07: Checked to age 70: past 70 waiting adds nothing and nearly everyone has claimed, so an unclaimed 73-to-85-year-old is not a household the population holds.

rules.check: if relation == 'spouse' (married) and both adults have birth years: for each spouse s with partner o where s.ssMode != 'none' and o has a figure (pia > 0): spousal = floorDime(max(0, o.pia/2 - s.pia) * spousalEarlyFactor(s.birthYear, startAge(s,o))); ASSERT ss.couple.spousalCounted[s] >= spousal - 0.1 whenever s.pia is 0 or unknown because s has no pay (status 'none', or 'work' with blank pay) AND ss.householdYearly >= 12*(o.monthly + max(s.monthly, s.monthly + spousal)) - 12 AND the projection counts it from max(62, both claim ages).
rules.threshold: at least the spousal benefit (32.5% to 50% of the partner's full-age amount), to the dime
rules.why: A husband or wife can get up to half of the worker's full-retirement amount, at least 32.5% if started at 62; SSA pays the larger of their own benefit and that one. Since January 2024 a government pension no longer cuts it (the Social Security Fairness Act ended the Government Pension Offset). A married stay-at-home spouse counted at $0 in retirement is impossible unless they said 'none'.
rules.source: SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, Benefits for Spouses, https://www.ssa.gov/oact/quickcalc/spouse.html ; SSA, Social Security Fairness Act, https://www.ssa.gov/benefits/retirement/social-security-fairness-act.html

When no pay history is known, the placeholder is a marked guess at the population figure: the average retired-worker benefit ($2,071 a month in January 2026; $2,170 from January 2027), or for a couple both receiving $3,208.

rules.why: 87.9% of Americans 65 and older received Social Security in December 2024 (lowest state, D.C., 74.8%); counting $0 for a retired person who did not say 'none' is outside the middle 90%.
rules.source: SSA, OASDI Beneficiaries by State and County, 2024, Table 1 (beneficiaries as a percentage of the population aged 65 or older), https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/statcomps/oasdi_sc/2024/table01.html ; SSA 2026 COLA fact sheet (average benefits after the COLA), https://www.ssa.gov/cola/factsheets/2026.html ; 2027 fact sheet https://www.ssa.gov/cola/factsheets/2027.html

rules.why: Left over each month is take-home minus spending and saving; if take-home is wrong (a state tax counted as $0, two partners on one return) the derived spending is wrong by the same amount. rules.check: for each adult a (age = ageOn(a.birthDate, today)) and each account r with r.ownerId == a.id, r.type in ['401k','ira','roth'] and a guess ledger entry on accounts[r.id].balance (keys account.retire.balance, account.ira.balance, account.retire.split): B = r.balance; pay = a's salary+bonus a year today (0 when retired or no pay); y = (pay > 0 ? min(pay, L402(age)) + 0.04*min(pay, 360000) : L402(age)) + IRA(age), where L402 = 24500 (+8000 from 50; +11250 instead at 60-63) and IRA = 7500 (+1100 from 50); n = ln(1 + 0.05*B/y) / ln(1.05) (years of putting in y at a 5% real return); ASSERT n <= max(0, age - 17). rules.threshold: implied years of saving <= adult years (age - 17, counting this year); 5% real return; today's pay as the ceiling for every past year
rules.why: The law caps what goes in each year: in 2026 a worker can defer at most $24,500 to a 401(k) ($32,500 from 50, $35,750 at 60-63), $7,500 to an IRA ($8,600 from 50), and all additions to one plan are capped at $72,000; Vanguard's median promised employer match is 4% of pay. A guessed balance that would take more years of the most a person can put in from today's pay than the person has been an adult cannot be the typical figure for them (it would need an inheritance or rollover nobody mentioned). This is the owner's 'a 25-year-old cannot hold decades of saving' made exact.

rules.threshold: IRS 2026 limits exactly; match never above what goes in or 6% of pay when guessed

rules.owner: leftover (the left-over input will feed L); the FIRE fix itself is not the leftover build's
rules.check: K = payroll retirement saving a year (sum of contributions taken from pay) + employer match; TH = take-home a year (cashflow/paycheck takeHome(plan).monthly * 12: after federal, state, Social Security and Medicare and the 401(k)); S = spending a year (cashflow/expenses monthly * 12, debt payments counted once); L = left over a year = TH - S (typed or derived once the 'leftover' build lands). For every page that states how much is saved a year or a saving rate (retirement/fire savingYearly and savingsRate, overview/health-score 'Saving each month', overview/next-best-action spare, cashflow/expenses savingsRate, the leftover build's yearly saving): ASSERT saved <= K + max(0, L) + $12 AND all of them state the same yearly figure within $12 (one figure across pages) AND a rate is that figure over one stated base (after-tax pay, or pay before tax), named on screen.
rules.threshold: $1 a month; saving never larger than take-home minus spending plus what goes in from pay
rules.why: Money can only be saved out of what reaches the bank and is not spent, plus what the employer and payroll put in before it arrives. Federal and state income tax and 7.65% Social Security and Medicare come off pay first. rules.check: for each adult a: R(a) = a.retirementAge ?? plan.assumptions.retirementAge (65); age(a) from a.birthDate. ASSERT a page states an age, years to retirement or a start year for a only when a.birthDate exists (no invented age: investments/glide-path ageNow, retirement/pensions ageNow, career/benefits life age 40, retirement/roth-conversions RMD age 75 fallback); ASSERT R(a) < planEnd(a) = a.lifeExpectancy ?? assumptions.planEndAge; for a retired adult (guide.setup.status == 'retired') years to retirement == 0 and no contribution is guessed; years to retirement = max(0, R(a) - age(a)) and the retirement year = birthYear + R(a) are the same on retirement/projection (inputs.people[i].retireAge, atRetirement.age for retireBy), retirement/fire, retirement/contributions, investments/glide-path, overview/timeline and scenarios/goal-seek. A worker already past R(a) is pt.pay.working-means-working.
rules.threshold: exact equality across pages; no age without a birth date
rules.why: 65 is the population's default for workers: in the 2026 Retirement Confidence Survey workers' median expected retirement age is 65 (retirees actually stopped at a median 62, and 46% earlier than planned). That makes 65 a fair placeholder for a worker with a birth date; an age of 45 or 60 for a person with no birth date is not drawn from anything about them.
rules.source: EBRI and Greenwald Research, 2026 Retirement Confidence Survey, Fact Sheet #2 'Expectations about retirement' (Figure 1 median ages; Figure 2 retired earlier than planned), https://www.ebri.org/docs/default-source/rcs/2026-rcs/rcs_26-fs-2.pdf
rules.skeptic: 2026-11-07: A retirement age past the plan's end is the person's own typed contradiction (qa plan-to-age-below-retirement), said on Assumptions, not a guess: only the cross-page equality is checked.

rules.check: for the household: E = planEnd of each adult (a.lifeExpectancy ?? assumptions.planEndAge, 95); x = today's age; single: p = l(E+1)/l(x) from the CDC 2024 life table by sex when known, else the total table; couple: p = 1 - (1 - p_a)(1 - p_b) (male and female tables when sexes unknown). ASSERT p <= 0.25 whenever E is a default (not typed); ASSERT E > x always (else no-years path).
rules.threshold: at most a 1-in-4 chance that the person (or one of the couple) is still alive the year after the plan ends
rules.why: Planning to 95 is right for most people: a 65-year-old has a 12% chance of reaching 95 (men 9%, women 15%) and for a couple of 65 the chance that one of them does is 22%. For the old it is not: a single 87-year-old has a 27% chance of reaching 95 and a 90-year-old 39%; for a couple aged 75 the chance that one is alive at 95 is 26%, at 85 it is 40%. A plan that ends while that many people like this are alive stops counting their money too soon.
rules.source: CDC/NCHS, United States Life Tables, 2024, National Vital Statistics Reports Vol. 75 No. 5, Tables 1-3 (l(x) survivors), https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr75/nvsr75-05.pdf ; spreadsheets https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Publications/NVSR/75-05/Table01.xlsx (02, 03). (SSA's period table at ssa.gov/oact refused the download: HTTP 403.)

rules.check: for each adult a with a birth date: startAge(a) = 70.5 if born before 1949-07-01; 72 if born 1949-07-01..1950-12-31; 73 if born 1951-1959; 75 if born 1960 or later; startYear = birthYear + startAge (70.5: +1 when born July-December). ASSERT retirement/rmd people[a].startAge/startYear, retirement/projection inputs.rmd.owners[i].startAge, retirement/roth-conversions rmdStartAge and the calendar/needs-attention deadline all equal these; a required withdrawal appears only in years with age >= startAge; only pre-tax accounts (401k, traditional IRA) count, never a Roth IRA, a designated Roth 401(k) (from 2024) or an HSA; amount(y) = prior 31 December pre-tax balance of that owner / Uniform Lifetime factor(age in y) (73: 26.5, 75: 24.6, 80: 20.2, 85: 16.0) within $1 when no spouse more than 10 years younger is the sole beneficiary; amount <= balance; first deadline 1 April of the year after startYear, later ones 31 December; an owner already past startAge with pre-tax money has this year's amount shown (> 0).
rules.threshold: exact (start age by birth year; factor from Table III; $1)
rules.why: SECURE 2.0 section 107 raised the required beginning age to 73 for those turning 72 after 2022 and to 75 for those turning 74 after 2032; the 2024 proposed regulations settle that people born in 1959 start at 73 and those born in 1960 or later at 75. The amount is the prior year-end balance over the Uniform Lifetime factor (26.5 at 73, 24.6 at 75). Roth IRAs and designated Roth accounts have no required withdrawals while the owner is alive.
rules.source: IRS Publication 590-B (2025), Appendix B Table III (Uniform Lifetime), https://www.irs.gov/publications/p590b ; IRS Retirement plan and IRA required minimum distributions FAQs, https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/retirement-plan-and-ira-required-minimum-distributions-faqs ; 2024 proposed RMD regulations on the 1959 birth year (summarised by PlanSponsor, 'IRS Proposes Regulations for Changes to SECURE 2.0 RMDs', https://www.plansponsor.com/irs-proposes-regulations-for-changes-to-secure-2-0-rmds/)
rules.sourceDate: Pub 590-B for 2025 returns (page reviewed 2026-04-30); FAQ reviewed 2026-01-29; proposed regulations July 2024

rules.check: pr = retirement/projection compute(plan, {today}). ASSERT pr.verdict in ['on track','tight','short']; (pr.verdict == 'short') == (pr.shortAge != null); if short: today's age < pr.shortAge <= planEnd; 'on track' => pr.affordable >= 1.15 * pr.spendingYearly; 'tight' => success and affordable < 1.15 * spending; pr.atRetirement.age == retirement age of pr.retireBy; and the same verdict and run-out age (or year) on savingVerdict(plan), overview/health-score 'Retirement on track', overview/dashboard, overview/quick answers, overview/timeline, overview/next-best-action and the 'Your plan' page. When any balance, contribution or spending figure the verdict uses is a guess, the page says the answer uses our guesses (core/estimate ledger).
rules.threshold: exact equality across pages
rules.why: One household has one answer to 'will the money last?'. Only 35% of non-retirees think their retirement saving is on track (SHED 2025), so a verdict is read closely; two pages giving different answers, or 'on track' next to a run-out age, makes the whole plan unbelievable.
rules.source: Federal Reserve Board, Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025 (SHED), 'Retirement and Investments' (35% of non-retirees think their retirement saving is on track), https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/2025-report-economic-well-being-us-households-202605.pdf

rules.check: For a household with a ready verdict: (1) +$10,000 on any retirement or investment balance; (2) -$100 a month on one spending row or on retirement.spendingMonthly; (3) +$100 a month on a contribution; (4) retirement age +1 for one adult while under 70. Re-run retirement/projection. ASSERT rank(verdict) never worsens (on track < tight < short) and the run-out age never comes earlier (none counts as later than any age); and (5) for two households identical but for a typed balance B1 < B2, verdict(B2) is not worse.
rules.threshold: never worse for more money, less spending or later retirement
rules.why: More savings, less spending or working longer cannot make the same money run out sooner; if it does, the engine is reacting to a table edge or a rounding, and the person would rightly stop trusting every number. (Pure logic; the population figures behind the inputs are in the rules above.)
rules.source: Internal consistency (no population figure needed); retirement engine core/math/retirement.js project()
rules.sourceDate: n/a
rules.knownCauses: Loans lane fix round 2 (2026-11-11, claude-c): 2 of 1,636 checks fail in the standard sweep, both '-$100 a month on a bill', neither a loan's: g252 (also on the base, renter, no loan) and g1392, where cutting one of Get started's guessed spending rows makes it typed and the other guessed rows are worked out again a little higher (Groceries $510 -> $540, Car $450 -> $480 ...), so the retirement figure rises $20 and the run-out age moves from 94 to 92. Fixed in that round: H-0329 (one mortgage whose bill was more than 10% off its payment was spent for life: cashflow/expenses debtsCounted) and g2244 (no longer fails).

rules.check: Same age sweep as sr.saving.monotone, every box blank (all guesses): for consecutive ages x, x+1 while working: ASSERT |rank(v(x+1)) - rank(v(x))| <= 1 AND, when both are 'short', |runOut(x+1) - runOut(x)| <= 3 years AND a run-out age appears or disappears between x and x+1 only when it lies within 3 years of the plan end.
rules.threshold: one year of age moves the run-out age by at most 3 years
rules.why: With nothing typed, the verdict rests on the guesses, and the guesses are typical balances, which grow smoothly with age (sr.saving.no-cliff). Being one year older with the same pay cannot move the year the money runs out by a decade: Vanguard's 2025 median 401(k) grows about 30% a year in the 20s, 10% a year in the 30s and 5% a year in the 40s, so a year of age moves typical savings by a fraction of a year's spending.
rules.source: Federal Reserve Board, 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances: Summary Extract Public Data (rscfp2025.dta in scfp2025s.zip; variables RETQLIQ, STOCKS, NMMF, LIQ, NETWORTH, INCOME, AGE, SAVED, WSAVED, WGT; all 5 implicates pooled, weighted percentiles worked out here, percentiles worked out from the public microdata for these rules), https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scfp2025s.zip ; Federal Reserve Bulletin 'Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025' (October 2026), Box 2 Table A, https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/scf26.pdf ; Vanguard, How America Saves 2026: Figure 53 (account balances by age and income, 2025), Figure 31 (deferral rates by age), Figure 30 (distribution of deferral rates), Figure 44 (total contribution rate), headline table (participation 83%, median promised match 4%), https://workplace.vanguard.com/content/dam/inst/iig-transformation/has/2026/pdf/HowAmericaSaves2026_accessibility.pdf

rules.check: For each debt d with a payment counted in retirement spending (overview/setup loansRunningThen / setupLoans, or Expenses' debtsCounted when spending is today's bills): payoff(d) = the payoff balance/liabilities shows: today + nper(rate/12, payment less the tax and insurance inside a mortgage's payment, owed) months (HD-PAYOFF-ONE-DATE). ASSERT in retirement/projection rows: the payment is part of spending only in years < payoff year, and as a fixed nominal amount (rows[y].spending/priceLevel falls by payment*12/priceLevel(y) after payoff); ASSERT no guessed loan is counted past the plan end.
rules.threshold: a loan's payment leaves retirement spending in its payoff year; nominal, not inflated
rules.why: A fixed-rate loan payment stops when the loan is paid and does not rise with inflation. Counting it in retirement spending for life, in today's dollars, adds money the household will never spend: for a 58-year-old couple it is $16,200 a year carried 23 years past payoff.
rules.source: Internal consistency with the app's own payoff date (core/math/finance.js nper; balance/liabilities payoff); Freddie Mac PMMS 30-year fixed-rate loans have a level payment, https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms

rules.check: E = goals/emergency-fund compute, Q = balance/liquidity compute, C = overview/setup cushion(plan, null, today). ASSERT E.target == Q.target == C.exact (within $1) and C.target == round(months * all must-pay bills on file, $100); E.months == Q.targetMonths in [3, 12] unless typed; E.runwayMonths == usable cash / must-pay monthly >= 0 (same on Liquidity, Dashboard, health score); E.readyDate >= this month when gap > 0; the cushion the guessed cash makes (months of must-pay bills) is the figure every page says.
rules.threshold: $1 across pages; months 3..12 when not typed
rules.why: The emergency fund is one number per household. The common measure is three months of expenses: in 2025, 55% of adults said they had set aside three months in a rainy-day fund and 63% would cover a $400 expense with cash.
rules.source: Federal Reserve Board, Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025 (SHED), 'Savings and Investments' (55% three months; 63% $400), https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/2025-report-economic-well-being-us-households-202605.pdf

rules.check: when plan.assumptions.emergencyMonths was never set by the person: ASSERT goals/emergency-fund months == suggestedMonths({ earners, variable, dependants }) (3 with two or more steady earners, 6 with one or none, +3 for pay that varies, at most 12), i.e. the target the page aims for equals the advice the same page gives; when typed, the page's warning appears only if typed < suggested.
rules.threshold: default months == the page's own suggested months
rules.why: Three months of expenses is the common yardstick (55% of adults have it, SHED 2025) and the page's own rule says 3 for two steady incomes, 6 for one. Aiming a two-earner couple at 6 months while the same page says 3 is the usual advice for them doubles the target from a default nobody chose.
rules.source: Federal Reserve Board, SHED 2025 (as above); modules/goals/emergency-fund README (suggestedMonths, 'the common 3-to-6-months advice')

rules.owner: bought (home value and mortgage owed are its guesses)
rules.check: N = balance/net-worth compute: ASSERT N.netWorth == N.assets - N.liabilities == sum over accounts (assets +, liabilities -) within $1; the same N.netWorth on overview/dashboard, balance/statement, overview/health-score and overview/timeline (today); retirement savings on Net worth (401k + ira + roth + hsa) == retirement/projection inputs.balances.deferred + free (minus hsa when the projection files it elsewhere) == retirement/rmd deferredNow + roth; a guessed liability never exceeds the asset it is tied to (HD-MORT-UNDERWATER, car loan vs car value).
rules.threshold: $1 across pages
rules.why: Net worth is assets minus debts, one figure per household on a given day. (The SCF 2025 median is $215,900 for all families and $33,000 under 35; a guessed figure is judged by its parts in sr.retire.like-you and sr.balance.like-you, since the whole is within the wide middle 90% for every household tried.)
rules.source: Federal Reserve Bulletin 'Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025' (October 2026), https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/scf26.pdf ; Federal Reserve Board, 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances: Summary Extract Public Data (rscfp2025.dta in scfp2025s.zip; variables RETQLIQ, STOCKS, NMMF, LIQ, NETWORTH, INCOME, AGE, SAVED, WSAVED, WGT; all 5 implicates pooled, weighted percentiles worked out here, percentiles worked out from the public microdata for these rules), https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scfp2025s.zip ; Federal Reserve Bulletin 'Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025' (October 2026), Box 2 Table A, https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/scf26.pdf

rules.check: When left over each month (L) is a guess (neither L nor spending typed) and household income I > 0: g = income group of I (SCF cut-offs $35,946 / $63,676 / $102,703 / $174,595 / $252,649); ASSERT L >= 0 and, for g in bottom 40%, L <= 0.05 * take-home (most such families spend all of income); for g in the top 40%, L > 0. When L is typed: spending shown = take-home - L - loan payments counted once (pt.leftover.identity) and yearly saving shown = 12*L + payroll saving + match (sr.saving.from-take-home). L is never shown as 'saved' when it is a derived guess.
rules.threshold: sign, and for the bottom 40% at most 25% of take-home (skeptic pass 2026-11-07; was: sign and size of a guessed left-over match the most common answer for the household's income group)
rules.why: Whether money is left over depends on income: in the SCF 2025, 30.8% of families in the bottom fifth of income spent less than their income over the year (29.1% spent more), 41.5% in the second fifth, 51.3% in the middle, 65.7% in the fourth fifth, 74.2% in the 80th-90th and 81.7% in the top tenth. In the SHED 2025, 41% of adults always or often have money left over at the end of the month: 20% with income under $25,000 and 59% with $100,000 or more. A default left-over is the most likely figure for that income.
rules.source: Federal Reserve Board, 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances: Summary Extract Public Data (rscfp2025.dta in scfp2025s.zip; variables RETQLIQ, STOCKS, NMMF, LIQ, NETWORTH, INCOME, AGE, SAVED, WSAVED, WGT; all 5 implicates pooled, weighted percentiles worked out here, percentiles worked out from the public microdata for these rules), https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/files/scfp2025s.zip ; Federal Reserve Bulletin 'Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025' (October 2026), Box 2 Table A, https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/scf26.pdf ; Federal Reserve Board, SHED 2025 Table 18 'How often have money left over at the end of the month (by family income)', https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/2025-report-economic-well-being-us-households-202605.pdf
rules.sourceDate: 2026-10-09 (summary extract posted; file dated 2026-10-05); Bulletin October 2026; 2026-05-13
rules.skeptic: 2026-11-07: Bottom 40%: up to 25% of take-home left over (5% failed common households, e.g. a $20,000 earner with $127 a month left); negative stays a failure (SF-LEFTOVER-DEFAULT has the floor).

rules.check: for k in kids with a birthDate, for a in adults with a birthDate: ASSERT k.birthDate > a.birthDate. for a in adults: ASSERT 15 <= age(a) <= 115. for p in people: ASSERT p.birthDate <= today. When a typed year breaks this, Get started's ages screen (applyAges) and People ask before saving ('Child 1 would be older than you. Is the year right?'), and until it is fixed no page treats that person as a child: no college years (goals/education children[]), no childcare price, not counted under 17 for the child tax credit (spend.js takeHome under17, taxes/federal), no years of income on Life cover, not the oldest child of the spending cell (spend.js householdOf).
rules.threshold: strict: every kid born after every adult; adults 15..115 years old; no birth date after today
rules.why: A child cannot be older than its parent. In 2024 only 1,727 of 3,628,934 U.S. births (0.05%) were to mothers younger than 15, and NCHS publishes birth rates only from age 10 (Table 2, '10-14'), so a birth child is always about 10 or more years younger than a parent. Census counts householders only from 15 (ACS table B25007's youngest band is 'Householder 15 to 24 years').
rules.source: CDC/NCHS, 'Births: Final Data for 2024', National Vital Statistics Reports vol. 75 no. 2, Table 3 (births by age of mother), https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr75/nvsr75-02.pdf; U.S. Census Bureau, ACS 2024 1-year, B25007 'Tenure by Age of Householder', https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs1/variables/B25007_003E.json
rules.sourceDate: NVSR dated 2026-06-09; read 2026-11-07; ACS variable label read 2026-11-07
rules.skeptic: 2026-11-07: A dependent of 18 or more can be a parent cared for at home (qa centenarian-dependent): only dependents under 18 must be born after every adult.

rules.check: for k in kids under 18 with a birthDate: atBirth(a) = year(k.birthDate) - year(a.birthDate) for each adult a with a birthDate; ASSERT exists a: 18 <= atBirth(a) <= 49. Otherwise the ages screen asks once, plainly ('You were 14 when Child 1 was born. Is that right?', with 'Yes, I look after them' as an answer) and never blocks; a 'yes' is kept and nothing is asked again.
rules.threshold: some adult 12 or more at the child's birth (skeptic pass 2026-11-07; was: some adult aged 18..49 at the child's birth (mothers: about the 1st and 99.7th percentiles; 49 leaves room for fathers))
rules.why: In 2024, 1.0% of births were to mothers under 18 (36,192 of 3,628,934: 1,727 under 15 and 34,465 aged 15-17) and 0.30% to mothers 45 or older (9,688 aged 45-49, 1,188 aged 50-54). A child whose every adult was under 18 or 50+ at the birth is most often a mistyped year, a grandchild or a sibling being raised, and the plan's child figures (college date, childcare, life cover years) should not rest on it unasked.
rules.source: CDC/NCHS, 'Births: Final Data for 2024', National Vital Statistics Reports vol. 75 no. 2, Table 3 (births by age of mother), https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr75/nvsr75-02.pdf
rules.skeptic: 2026-11-07: Children's birth years are always typed, never guessed, and an adult of 50+ at the birth is often a grandparent raising the child (Census: about 2.4 million grandparents responsible for grandchildren): only a gap no family can have (under 12) is flagged.

rules.check: for d in dependents with no birthDate: youngest = min age(a) over adults with a birthDate. IF youngest >= 63: the pages take d as an adult dependent: not under 17 for the child tax credit (spend.js takeHome under17; taxes/federal), not 'couple with children' or 'one parent' for the spending cell (householdOf), no childcare row, no college; the why-line says so and asks for the age (sharperWith 'your children's ages'). IF youngest < 63: a child of unknown age stays a minor (as now). Same rule on every page (see SF-FAM-CHILD-AGES-ONE-SOURCE).
rules.threshold: youngest adult 63 or older (45 + 18: a dependent under 18 would need a mother of 45+ at the birth, 0.30% of births)
rules.why: The likeliest age of an undated dependent follows from the adults' ages: births to mothers 45 or older were 0.30% of 2024 births, so a dependent of a couple in their 60s or 70s is almost always an adult (a grown child, a parent). The child tax credit is up to $2,200 per child who is under 17 at the end of the year (IRS, tax year 2025), a real sum to count by default.
rules.source: CDC/NCHS, 'Births: Final Data for 2024', National Vital Statistics Reports vol. 75 no. 2, Table 3 (births by age of mother), https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr75/nvsr75-02.pdf; IRS, Child Tax Credit, https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/individuals/child-tax-credit
rules.sourceDate: NVSR dated 2026-06-09; read 2026-11-07; IRS page last reviewed 2026-10-29, read 2026-11-07
rules.skeptic: 2026-11-07: The CE 'married couple with children, Total' cell holds children of any age (an adult child at home): it is allowed.

rules.check: for k in kids with a birthDate, every page uses age(k) from that one date at the same today: Education startYear = year(birthDate) + startAge, first bill Aug 15 of startYear; childcare bucket by age(k) (0 infant, 1-2 toddler, 3-5 four-year-old, 6-12 before/after school, 13+ none); the child tax credit counts k while under 17; Life cover's years of income = max(0, 18 - exact age of the youngest kid) (insurance/life-needs dime.incomeYears) and its college = Education's figure for each kid under 18; the spending cell by the oldest kid (<6, 6-17, 18+); the education goal date (SF-GOAL-EDU). Moving a birth year on People moves all of them at the next render.
rules.threshold: exact (Life cover years to the month)
rules.why: One child, one age: two pages that disagree about the same child are wrong on one of them. The care price stops at 13, the age the dependent care credit uses ('under age 13 when the care was provided', IRS Pub. 503); the child tax credit stops at 17 (IRS).
rules.source: IRS Publication 503 (2025), https://www.irs.gov/publications/p503 ; IRS Child Tax Credit, https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/individuals/child-tax-credit
rules.sourceDate: Pub. 503 for 2025 returns; IRS CTC page reviewed 2026-10-29; both read 2026-11-07

rules.check: (a) every goal date written or derived with no date typed is after today: setup GOALS years (home 3, education 10, trip 1, car 3, other 2; applyGoalDetails, compute.js:1596) and Education's 'Make it the child's goal' date; (b) Education's startAge (whatIfs.college[id].startAge) is 14..30, so startYear >= year(birthDate) + 14; outside, the box refuses it with a plain message and nothing is priced; (c) a goal with saved < target and targetDate < today reads 'past due', computes no monthly figure over <= 0 months (goals/goals neededMonthly null) and asks for a new date; (d) no goal or college year is dated before the person it is for was born.
rules.threshold: every default date > today; startAge 14..30; no date before the person's birth
rules.why: A goal dated in the past cannot be saved for, and full college years cannot begin at 5. The youngest college students are counted as 'under 18' (1,487,087 of 15,447,557 in fall 2021, mostly high-school students taking college classes), so 14 is a floor no real plan goes under.
rules.source: NCES, Digest of Education Statistics 2023, Table 303.50 'Total fall enrollment in degree-granting postsecondary institutions, by ... age of student: 2021', https://nces.ed.gov/programs/digest/d23/tables/dt23_303.50.asp
rules.sourceDate: Digest 2023 table (fall 2021 data); read 2026-11-07

rules.check: IF kids under 18 with a birthDate exist AND Get started writes setup-goal-education with no date typed: target year = year(birthDate) + 18 of the oldest kid under 18 whose college has not begun, dated at Education's first fall bill (Aug 15), never today + 10. ASSERT |year(goal.targetDate) - education.children[k].startYear| <= 1 AND goal.targetDate > today. With no kid under 18 (the adult's own schooling) a future default stays. Education with nothing typed: yearly cost = College Board public four-year in-state published price (tuition and fees + housing and food) grown at its rate; ASSERT within [public two-year with housing, private nonprofit] of the same year; years = 4, allowed 1..6.
rules.threshold: goal year within 1 of the child's first college year; 2025-26 cost $15,000..$60,920 a year (default $25,850); years 1..6
rules.why: 62% of high-school completers are enrolled in college in the October right after (NCES, 2022), so the fall after a child turns 18 is the likeliest start, and it is what the Education page already uses (DEFAULTS startAge 18). Published 2025-26 prices: public four-year in-state $11,950 + $13,900 = $25,850; public two-year $4,150 + $10,850 = $15,000; private nonprofit $45,000 + $15,920 = $60,920.
rules.source: NCES, Condition of Education, 'Immediate College Enrollment Rate', https://nces.ed.gov/programs/coe/indicator/cpa/immediate-college-enrollment-rate ; College Board, Trends in College Pricing and Student Aid 2025 (Table CP-1 and the budget figure), https://research.collegeboard.org/media/pdf/Trends-in-College-Pricing-and-Student-Aid-2025-final_0.pdf
rules.sourceDate: NCES page last updated May 2024 (2022 data); College Board report 2025 (2025-26 prices); both read 2026-11-07

rules.check: walk(H) with nothing typed: S = TOTAL - G.housing for a renter (the survey leaves rent out), TOTAL for an owner (home costs besides the mortgage are in; loan payments are not in TOTAL). ASSERT SCF_TOT[fam][fifth].p5 <= S <= SCF_TOT[fam][fifth].p95. The same band holds for a spending month worked out from a typed left over (SF-LEFTOVER-TYPED); outside it the page says the two do not fit.
